newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Japanese emperor begins Brazil visit in the Amazon.
newsitem.headline: Japanese emperor begins Brazil visit in the Amazon.

text.p: Japanese Emperor Akihito and Empress Michiko began a two-week official visit to Brazil and Argentina on Sunday with a boat trip near the mouth of the Amazon River and a meeting with the local Japanese community.

The imperial couple, accompanied by about 70 Japanese and Brazilian officials and journalists, spent the morning cruising on the Guama River, which flows into the Amazon at Belem, the colonial capital of Para state.

The state, one of the biggest in Brazil, is predominantly covered by rainforest. Once one of the world's biggest rubber producers, Para's main industry is logging; large areas of the forest in the south of the state have been cleared.

Later, in a speech during an official lunch, Akihito spoke of his interest in the local environment and, in particular, the acai palm trees which sustain jungle settlers with their nutritious berries.
"I profoundly desire that the state of Para state, which is blessed with the Amazon River and lush nature, can develop in harmony with the environment," the emperor said.
He and Empress Michiko then met about 600 representatives of the roughly 100,000 descendents of Japanese immigrants living in Para.
In the 1950s, the immigrants set up successful black pepper farms in the forest. Those farms produce a wide range of tropical fruits which are exported worldwide.
The imperial couple was due to fly to the capital, Brasilia, on Monday for an audience with President Fernando Henrique Cardoso.

"(The emperor's) visit is unquestionable proof of Japan's appreciation and friendship and eloquently illustrates the excellent relations between our counties," Cardoso wrote in an article published in the newspaper Correio Braziliense.
Akihito and Michiko were also to visit the cities of Belo Horizonte, Sao Paulo, Curitiba and Rio de Janeiro; they were to meet representatives of local Japanese communities in each place.

Immigrants from Japan began arriving in Brazil at the turn of the century, attracted by the country's coffee and agricultural boom. Now numbering about 1.3 million, they represent the biggest overseas Japanese community.
About 200,000 Brazilians of Japanese descent are currently working in Japan and the money they send home represents an appreciable source of income for the South American country.

As well as their historic ties, Brazil and Japan are important trade partners with $6.5 billion of business done between the two countries in 1995. Japan also provides Brazil with technical and financial assistance for agricultural, energy and environmental projects.
The emperor and empress were due to fly to Buenos Aires June 9 for a three-day visit to Argentina.

Throughout their trip, the imperial couple will be protected by Japanese police rather than the imperial guards normally used on foreign visits. The measure was seen as a sign of security concerns in Japan after the four-month hostage drama at the Japanese ambassador's residence in Peru.

Brazilian newspaper O Globo also reported on Sunday that 60 Japanese anti-terrorist police arrived in Brazil in April and May, posing as tourists and businessmen but seeking to uncover any possible plot against the imperial couple.
